text: (a) What are isotopes? (b) Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties but different physical properties?
modelAnswer: (a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number (same number of protons) but different mass numbers (different number of neutrons). Example: ¹₁H, ²₁H, ³₁H, or ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C. (b) Chemical properties depend on the number of electrons, especially valence electrons. Isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, so they react the same way. Physical properties such as mass, density, melting and boiling points depend on the mass of the atom. Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses, so their physical properties differ.
keyPoints: Same atomic number, different mass number
Same electronic configuration gives same chemical properties
Different number of neutrons gives different mass and physical properties

text: State one point of difference between: (a) an atom and an ion; (b) the duplet rule and the octet rule.
modelAnswer: (a) An atom is electrically neutral because its number of protons equals its number of electrons. An ion carries a positive or negative charge because it has lost or gained electrons, so its electrons do not equal its protons (e.g. Na has 11 electrons, Na⁺ has 10). (b) Duplet rule: an atom becomes stable with 2 electrons in its only (K) shell, like helium. This applies to H, Li and Be. Octet rule: an atom becomes stable with 8 electrons in its outermost shell, like neon or argon.
keyPoints: Duplet: 2 electrons in outer shell (He configuration)

text: An element has 2 electrons in its fourth shell. State: (i) its electronic configuration; (ii) whether it is a metal or a non-metal; (iii) its valency; (iv) the general name of the elements of the group it belongs to.
modelAnswer: (i) The element fills K, L and M first: 2, 8, 8, 2. This is Calcium, atomic number 20. (In ICSE Class IX the 3d shell is not filled before 4s.) (ii) It is a metal, because it has 2 valence electrons which it loses easily. (iii) Its valency is 2. It loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺. (iv) It belongs to Group 2, the alkaline earth metals.

text: Five atoms are labelled A to E with mass numbers and atomic numbers: A (40, 20), B (19, 9), C (7, 3), D (16, 8), E (14, 7). Which atom: (a) has 20 neutrons in the nucleus; (b) has electronic configuration 2,7; (c) Write the formula of the compound formed between C and D, and state the type of bond.
modelAnswer: (a) A has 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons. (b) B has atomic number 9, so its configuration is 2,7 (Fluorine). (c) C has atomic number 3, so it is Lithium (2,1) with valency 1. D has atomic number 8, so it is Oxygen (2,6) with valency 2. Two Li atoms each give 1 electron to one O atom, so the formula is C₂D, i.e. Li₂O. The bond is ionic (electrovalent).

text: The mass numbers and electronic configurations of five elements are: A (9; 2,2), B (19; 2,7), C (23; 2,8,1), D (28; 2,8,4), E (40; 2,8,8). (a) Name the element which has 22 neutrons. (b) What is the atomic number of C? (c) Write the formula of the compound forming the most stable ionic bond. (d) Write the formula of the compound between B and D.
modelAnswer: Atomic numbers come from the configurations: A = 4 (Be), B = 9 (F), C = 11 (Na), D = 14 (Si), E = 18 (Ar). (a) E has 40 − 18 = 22 neutrons, so the element is Argon. (b) The atomic number of C is 11 (Sodium). (c) The most stable ionic bond forms between the most electropositive metal, C (Na, loses 1 e⁻), and the most electronegative non-metal, B (F, gains 1 e⁻). The compound is CB, i.e. NaF. (d) D (Si) has valency 4 and B (F) has valency 1, so the formula is DB₄, i.e. SiF₄. This is a covalent compound in which Si shares one electron pair with each F.

text: Element X has two valence electrons in its M shell. In element Y, electrons are distributed in the first three shells and Y has eight electrons in its M shell. Element Z has eight electrons in its penultimate shell (M), and its valence shell has fewer electrons than its first shell. (a) Give the electronic configuration of X. (b) Which element among X, Y, Z is inert? (c) In which atom are electrons distributed in all four shells? (d) What is the atomic number of Z? (e) How many electrons and protons are present in Y?
modelAnswer: (a) X has 2 electrons in the M (third) shell as its valence shell, so X = 2,8,2 (Magnesium, Z = 12). (b) Y = 2,8,8 (Argon), which has a complete octet, so Y is inert. (c) Z has M as its penultimate shell, so it has a fourth (N) shell. The first shell holds 2 electrons, so Z's valence shell has fewer than 2, i.e. 1 electron. Z = 2,8,8,1 (Potassium), and Z is the atom with electrons in all four shells. (d) The atomic number of Z is 2 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 19. (e) Y has 18 electrons and 18 protons.

text: Study the table: P (mass number 12, neutrons 6), Q (20, 10), R (23, 12), S (35, 18). (i) Write the atomic number of S. (ii) Write the electronic configuration of R. (iii) To which group does Q belong? (iv) What type of compound (ionic or covalent) is formed by (A) R and S, (B) P and S?
modelAnswer: Atomic number = mass number − neutrons. P = 6 (Carbon), Q = 10 (Neon), R = 11 (Sodium), S = 17 (Chlorine). (i) The atomic number of S is 35 − 18 = 17. (ii) R has atomic number 11, so its configuration is 2,8,1. (iii) Q = 2,8 (Neon) belongs to Group 18 (0), the noble gases. (iv) (A) R (Na, a metal) and S (Cl, a non-metal) form an ionic compound, NaCl, by transfer of an electron. (B) P (C) and S (Cl) are both non-metals, so they form a covalent compound, CCl₄, by sharing electrons.
keyPoints: R + S: ionic (NaCl); P + S: covalent (CCl₄)

text: Differentiate between a group and a period of the periodic table (definition).
modelAnswer: Group: a vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. The modern table has 18 groups. Period: a horizontal row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells, and their properties change gradually across the period. There are 7 periods.
keyPoints: Group: vertical column, same valence electrons, similar properties
Period: horizontal row, same number of shells

text: Study the extract of the periodic table (letters are not the actual symbols). Period 1: A (Group 1), H (Group 18). Period 2: C (Group 13), D (Group 14), E (Group 15), P (Group 16). Period 3: B (Group 1), G (Group 17), F (Group 18). Period 4: Q (Group 18). State which element: (a) forms an electrovalent compound with G; (b) is non-metallic and has a valency of 2; (c) is an inert gas; (d) is the most non-metallic element in the given table; (e) What type of bond is present in a molecule of G?
modelAnswer: Identities: A = H, H = He, C = B (boron), D = C (carbon), E = N, P = O, B = Na, G = Cl, F = Ar, Q = Kr. (a) B (sodium, a Group 1 metal) gives its single valence electron to G (chlorine) and forms the electrovalent compound BG (NaCl). (b) P (oxygen, Group 16, configuration 2,6) is a non-metal with valency 2. (c) H, F or Q (He, Ar, Kr). All are Group 18 inert gases. (d) G (chlorine, Group 17). Halogens are the most non-metallic, readily gaining one electron. (e) G₂ (Cl₂) has a single covalent bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons.
keyPoints: P (O) is a non-metal with valency 2
H, F, Q are inert gases
G₂ has a single covalent bond

text: A periodic arrangement compares elements to the notes of music (sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni). (a) Name the scientist who proposed this periodic table. (b) Did this system work well for the heavier or the lighter elements? (c) What is the significance of the musical notes in this table?
modelAnswer: (a) John Newlands, through his Law of Octaves (1866). (b) It worked well only for the lighter elements, up to calcium. After calcium the pattern broke down, and it had no place for noble gases discovered later. (c) Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of atomic mass. He found that every eighth element had properties similar to the first, just as the eighth note in a musical scale repeats the first (sa … sa). The musical notes show this repetition of properties at every eighth element.
keyPoints: Worked only for lighter elements (up to calcium)
Every eighth element resembles the first, like musical octaves

text: With reference to Mendeleev's periodic table: (a) What was the basis of classification? (b) Which group of elements was not known at that time? (c) Why was the table later replaced (state its main drawbacks)?
modelAnswer: (a) Elements were arranged in increasing order of atomic weight (atomic mass), with elements of similar properties placed in the same group. (b) The noble gases (Group 18 / zero group) had not been discovered. (c) Main drawbacks: (i) Isotopes have different atomic masses but would need different places, yet they are the same element. (ii) In some places the order of atomic mass had to be broken, e.g. Co (58.9) before Ni (58.7) and Ar before K. (iii) Hydrogen had no fixed position. (iv) Chemically dissimilar elements were placed together. After Moseley showed that atomic number is more fundamental, the table was replaced by the Modern (long form) Periodic Table based on atomic number.
keyPoints: Anomalies: isotopes, Co/Ni, Ar/K, position of hydrogen
Replaced by Modern Periodic Table based on atomic number

text: Based on the periodic table: A (atomic no. 11), B (12), C (14), E (16), F (17), G (18) all lie in one period. (i) Give the period number of C. (ii) Give the configuration of the element that would be directly above A. (iii) What is the name of the elements of Group 17 (VIIA) and what does the name mean? (iv) Why is the placement of G in this period logical?
modelAnswer: (i) C has atomic number 14 (2,8,4), with 3 shells, so it is in Period 3. (ii) A is sodium (2,8,1). The element above it in Group 1 is lithium, configuration 2,1. (iii) Group 17 elements are called halogens, which means 'salt producers'. They react with metals to form salts such as NaCl. (iv) G has atomic number 18 (2,8,8), argon. It has 3 shells, so it belongs to Period 3, and its outer shell is a complete octet, so it ends the period as a noble gas in Group 18.
keyPoints: G = Ar (2,8,8): 3 shells, complete octet, ends Period 3

text: Match the atomic numbers 4, 8, 10, 15 and 19 with each of the following: (a) an element which can form a trivalent ion; (b) an element with 4 shells; (c) an element with 6 valence electrons; (d) an element which does not form an ion; (e) an element that belongs to the alkaline earth metals group.
modelAnswer: Configurations: 4 = 2,2 (Be); 8 = 2,6 (O); 10 = 2,8 (Ne); 15 = 2,8,5 (P); 19 = 2,8,8,1 (K). (a) 15 (P): it gains 3 electrons to form P³⁻. (b) 19 (K): 2,8,8,1 has 4 shells. (c) 8 (O): 2,6. (d) 10 (Ne): it has a complete octet, so it is inert. (e) 4 (Be): 2,2, Group 2.

text: (a) Name a stable negative ion which has the same electronic configuration as argon. (b) Write the period and group of the element with atomic number 3. (c) Similar chemical properties are seen for elements in the periodic table at regular intervals. What is the reason for this pattern?
modelAnswer: (a) Chloride ion, Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Also S²⁻ (sulphide) or P³⁻. (b) Atomic number 3 is lithium (2,1): Period 2, Group 1 (IA). (c) Chemical properties depend on the number of valence electrons. When elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, the same outer-shell configuration recurs at regular intervals (after 2, 8, 8, 18 … elements). Elements with the same number of valence electrons therefore show similar properties. This is periodicity.
keyPoints: Cl⁻ (or S²⁻) is isoelectronic with Ar

text: Give reasons: (a) Alkali metals are strong reducing agents. (b) Noble gases do not combine with other elements to form molecules. (c) Halogens are good oxidising agents. (d) Alkali metals and halogens do not occur free in nature.
modelAnswer: (a) Alkali metals have only one valence electron and low ionisation energy, so they lose that electron very easily. A substance that donates electrons is a reducing agent. (b) Noble gases have a stable, completely filled outer shell (an octet, or a duplet for He). They have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, so they have zero valency and do not form molecules. (c) Halogens have 7 valence electrons, high electronegativity and high electron affinity, so they readily gain one electron to complete their octet. A substance that accepts electrons is an oxidising agent. (d) Both are extremely reactive: alkali metals lose an electron easily and halogens gain one easily. They therefore always occur combined in compounds such as NaCl and KCl, not as free elements.
keyPoints: Alkali metals: 1 valence electron, easily lost → reducing
Noble gases: complete octet/duplet → zero valency
High reactivity → occur only in compounds

text: Draw electron dot diagrams for the formation of: (a) Magnesium chloride [Mg = 12, Cl = 17] (b) Water molecule [H = 1, O = 8] (c) Methane [C = 6, H = 1]
modelAnswer: (a) MgCl₂ (ionic). Mg (2,8,2) loses its 2 valence electrons, one to each of two Cl atoms (2,8,7). Diagram: Mg with two crosses (×) in its outer shell. Each × moves to a different Cl, which has 7 dots, giving [Mg]²⁺ and 2[:Cl:]⁻, each Cl⁻ with 8 electrons (7 dots + 1 cross). Mg²⁺ has the neon configuration (2,8) and each Cl⁻ the argon configuration (2,8,8). (b) H₂O (covalent). O (2,6) shares one electron pair with each of two H atoms. Diagram: H ×• O •× H, with two more lone pairs (4 dots) on O. O now has 8 electrons (2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs), each H has 2 (duplet), and there are 2 single covalent bonds. (c) CH₄ (covalent). C (2,4) shares one electron pair with each of four H atoms. Diagram: C at the centre with 4 shared pairs (•×) to H atoms above, below, left and right. C has an octet, each H a duplet, and there are 4 single covalent bonds with no lone pairs on C.
keyPoints: MgCl₂: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; each Cl gains 1e⁻ → Cl⁻ (ionic)
H₂O: 2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs on O (covalent)
CH₄: 4 shared pairs, octet on C, duplet on each H

text: Draw electron dot structures for the formation of: (a) Calcium oxide [Ca = 20, O = 8] (b) Carbon tetrachloride [C = 6, Cl = 17] (c) Oxygen molecule
modelAnswer: (a) CaO (ionic). Ca (2,8,8,2) transfers its 2 valence electrons to O (2,6), giving [Ca]²⁺ [:O:]²⁻. O²⁻ has 8 outer electrons (6 dots + 2 crosses), the neon configuration, and Ca²⁺ has the argon configuration (2,8,8). (b) CCl₄ (covalent). C (2,4) shares one electron pair with each of four Cl atoms (2,8,7). Each Cl keeps 3 lone pairs and gains a share of one pair, so it has an octet. C has an octet with 4 bond pairs. There are 4 single covalent bonds. (c) O₂ (covalent). Each O (2,6) needs 2 electrons, so the two O atoms share two pairs of electrons, a double bond (O=O). Each O keeps 2 lone pairs, so each has an octet (2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs).
keyPoints: CCl₄: 4 single covalent bonds, 3 lone pairs on each Cl
O₂: double covalent bond (O=O), 2 lone pairs on each O

text: (a) Draw the orbit structure for the formation of a nitrogen molecule. (b) What is meant by a 'lone pair of electrons'? Show the lone pairs in an orbit (electron dot) diagram of a water molecule.
modelAnswer: (a) Nitrogen (2,5) needs 3 more electrons. Two N atoms each contribute 3 electrons and share 3 pairs, forming a triple covalent bond, N≡N. Each N keeps 1 lone pair and has an octet (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair). (b) A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom only and is not shared in bond formation. In H₂O, oxygen (6 valence electrons) uses 2 electrons to form two O–H bond pairs (H ×• O •× H). Its remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, drawn as two pairs of dots on O. Water therefore has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs.
keyPoints: N₂: 3 shared pairs (triple bond), 1 lone pair on each N
Lone pair: valence electron pair not involved in bonding
H₂O: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs on oxygen

text: A compound has the formula H₂Y, where Y is a non-metal with 2 energy levels. State: (i) the electronic configuration of Y; (ii) the valency of Y; (iii) the type of bonding in H₂Y; (iv) the formula of the compound formed between calcium and Y.
modelAnswer: Y forms H₂Y, so it has valency 2. A non-metal with 2 shells and valency 2 is oxygen. (i) The configuration of Y is 2,6. (ii) The valency of Y is 2, since it needs 2 electrons to complete its octet. (iii) H₂Y (H₂O) has covalent bonding. Y shares one electron pair with each H atom. (iv) Calcium (valency 2) and Y (valency 2) combine 1:1, so the formula is CaY (CaO), an ionic compound.

text: Using only the ions Al³⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻, Ag⁺, OH⁻, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, S²⁻, CO₃²⁻, Hg²⁺, O²⁻ and Fe³⁺, give formulae for: (a) a nitrate P of a metal that decomposes on heating to give a solid residue and oxygen gas only; (b) a salt Q that decomposes in the presence of sunlight; (c) salt R formed when aluminium reacts with a greenish-yellow gas; (d) alkali S formed when sodium oxide is added to water; (e) salt T which on heating gives a metal used in thermometers, carbon dioxide and oxygen.
modelAnswer: (a) P = KNO₃. Nitrates of very reactive metals give the nitrite and oxygen only: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂. (b) Q = AgCl. It undergoes photochemical decomposition: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight). (c) R = AlCl₃. The greenish-yellow gas is chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. (d) S = NaOH: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH. (e) T = HgCO₃. Mercury is the thermometer metal: 2HgCO₃ → 2Hg + 2CO₂ + O₂.

text: Balance the following equations: (i) Cu(NO₃)₂ → CuO + NO₂ + O₂ (on heating) (ii) FeS₂ + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ (on heating) (iii) H₂S + O₂ → H₂O + SO₂ (iv) KMnO₄ + HCl → KCl + MnCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂
modelAnswer: (i) 2Cu(NO₃)₂ → 2CuO + 4NO₂ + O₂. (ii) 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂. (iii) 2H₂S + 3O₂ → 2H₂O + 2SO₂. (iv) 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂. Check for (iv): K 2 = 2; Mn 2 = 2; O 8 = 8; H 16 = 16; Cl 16 = 2 + 4 + 10.

text: Balance the following equations: (a) S + H₂SO₄ → SO₂ + H₂O (b) Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂ (c) P + HNO₃ → NO₂ + H₂O + H₃PO₄ (d) Pb₃O₄ + HCl → PbCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂ (e) (NH₄)₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → NH₃ + H₂O + CaSO₄
modelAnswer: (a) S + 2H₂SO₄ → 3SO₂ + 2H₂O. (b) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (c) P + 5HNO₃ → 5NO₂ + H₂O + H₃PO₄. Check: H 5 = 2 + 3; N 5 = 5; O 15 = 10 + 1 + 4. (d) Pb₃O₄ + 8HCl → 3PbCl₂ + 4H₂O + Cl₂. (e) (NH₄)₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NH₃ + 2H₂O + CaSO₄.

text: Balance the following equations: (a) Cu + HNO₃ (dilute) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + NO (b) Ca(OH)₂ + P₄O₁₀ → CaHPO₄ + H₂O (c) CuO + NH₃ → Cu + N₂ + H₂O (d) PbO₂ + HCl → PbCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂
modelAnswer: (a) 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO. Check: N 8 = 6 + 2; O 24 = 18 + 4 + 2. (b) 4Ca(OH)₂ + P₄O₁₀ → 4CaHPO₄ + 2H₂O. Check: O 18 = 16 + 2; H 8 = 4 + 4. (c) 3CuO + 2NH₃ → 3Cu + N₂ + 3H₂O. (d) PbO₂ + 4HCl → PbCl₂ + 2H₂O + Cl₂.

text: Balance the following equations: (i) Cu + HNO₃ (conc.) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + NO₂ (ii) HNO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O (iii) Na₂CO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (iv) Zn + AgNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + Ag (v) Al + CuCl₂ → AlCl₃ + Cu
modelAnswer: (i) Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂. (ii) 2HNO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O. (iii) Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. (iv) Zn + 2AgNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. (v) 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu.

text: Balance the following equations: (1) FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → FeCl₃ (2) Pb(OH)₂ + HCl → H₂O + PbCl₂ (3) Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂ (4) HNO₃ + NaHCO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ (5) H₂O + O₂ → H₂O₂ (6) Fe + HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + NO₂
modelAnswer: (1) 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. (2) Pb(OH)₂ + 2HCl → 2H₂O + PbCl₂. (3) 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. (4) HNO₃ + NaHCO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, which is already balanced. (5) 2H₂O + O₂ → 2H₂O₂. (6) Fe + 4HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂. Check: N 4 = 2 + 2; O 12 = 6 + 2 + 4.

text: Write balanced equations for the conversions: PbO → (A) → Pb(NO₃)₂; Pb(NO₃)₂ → (B) → PbSO₄; Pb(NO₃)₂ → (C) → Pb(OH)₂.
modelAnswer: A: PbO + 2HNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + H₂O. A basic oxide is neutralised by an acid. B: Pb(NO₃)₂ + H₂SO₄ → PbSO₄↓ + 2HNO₃. Na₂SO₄ also works: Pb(NO₃)₂ + Na₂SO₄ → PbSO₄↓ + 2NaNO₃. White insoluble lead sulphate precipitates. C: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2NaOH → Pb(OH)₂↓ + 2NaNO₃. White lead hydroxide precipitates (it dissolves in excess NaOH, being amphoteric, so the alkali is added dropwise).

text: Write balanced equations for: (i) a divalent metal reacting with a yellow non-metal to form an insoluble salt; (ii) thermal decomposition of silver (I) nitrate; (iii) conversion of a soluble salt of lead to an insoluble salt of lead; (iv) a trivalent metal reacting with a blue copper salt solution; (v) a weak alkali treated with a dilute acid to give a sublimable solid and water.
modelAnswer: (i) Fe + S → FeS (on heating). Sulphur is the yellow non-metal and iron(II) sulphide is insoluble. Zn + S → ZnS is also acceptable. (ii) 2AgNO₃ → 2Ag + 2NO₂ + O₂. (iii) Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2NaCl → PbCl₂↓ + 2NaNO₃. (iv) 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu. (v) NH₄OH + HCl → NH₄Cl + H₂O. Ammonium chloride sublimes.

text: Give balanced equations for: (a) a direct combination reaction between phosphorus and oxygen; (b) conversion of zinc nitrate to insoluble zinc carbonate by double decomposition; (c) neutralisation of lead hydroxide by nitric acid; (d) magnesium reacting with nitrogen gas; (e) strong heating of anhydrous copper sulphate.
modelAnswer: (a) P₄ + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀. Burning phosphorus in excess oxygen gives phosphorus pentoxide. (b) Zn(NO₃)₂ + Na₂CO₃ → ZnCO₃↓ + 2NaNO₃. (c) Pb(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O. (d) 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ (on heating). (e) CuSO₄ → CuO + SO₃ (strong heat). The black residue is CuO.

text: Complete and balance the following equations: (a) Al + H₂O + NaOH → (b) ZnSO₄ + (NH₄)₂CO₃ → (c) NH₄OH + HCl →
modelAnswer: (a) 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂. Sodium aluminate forms and hydrogen is evolved. (b) ZnSO₄ + (NH₄)₂CO₃ → ZnCO₃↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄. This is double decomposition with a white precipitate of zinc carbonate. (c) NH₄OH + HCl → NH₄Cl + H₂O. This is neutralisation.

text: A solid A on heating erupts like a volcano to form a compound B and two gases. One of the gases condenses to a neutral colourless liquid. (a) Identify and name A and B. (b) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (c) State the colour change observed.
modelAnswer: (a) A is ammonium dichromate, (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇. B is chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃. (b) (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ → Cr₂O₃ + N₂ + 4H₂O. The steam condenses to water, the neutral colourless liquid, and the other gas is nitrogen. (c) The orange crystals change to a voluminous green powder (Cr₂O₃), with sparks, like a volcano.
keyPoints: A = ammonium dichromate; B = chromium(III) oxide

text: An iron nail is placed in copper sulphate solution. (i) Identify the type of reaction. (ii) Identify the light green solution formed. (iii) What is the pink (reddish-brown) deposit seen after the reaction? (iv) Give the balanced equation.
modelAnswer: (i) It is a displacement reaction (single displacement), because iron is more reactive than copper. (ii) The light green solution is iron(II) sulphate (ferrous sulphate), FeSO₄. (iii) The pink deposit is copper metal. (iv) Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. The blue colour of CuSO₄ fades to light green.

text: Write equations and identify A–F: (i) A light green salt of copper decomposes on heating to give a black basic oxide A and an acidic gas B. (ii) A reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give a soluble salt C and water. (iii) On strong heating, C gives an oxide, an acidic gas D and oxygen. (iv) Adding sodium hydroxide solution to C gives a pale blue precipitate E and a soluble salt. (v) B reacts with water to form an acid F.
modelAnswer: The light green salt is copper carbonate, CuCO₃. (i) CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂, so A = CuO (black) and B = CO₂. (ii) CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O, so C = CuSO₄ (blue solution). (iii) 2CuSO₄ → 2CuO + 2SO₂ + O₂ (strong heat), so D = SO₂. (iv) CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄, so E = Cu(OH)₂ (pale blue precipitate). (v) CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, so F = carbonic acid.

text: Viaan heated a blue crystalline salt P. It first gave water vapour and an anhydrous white salt X. On strong heating, X gave a black residue, a colourless neutral gas and an acidic gas that turns acidified potassium dichromate solution clear green. A solution of X gave a blue insoluble precipitate with sodium hydroxide. (a) Name the acidic gas evolved on strong heating. (b) Write a balanced equation for the strong heating of X. (c) Identify P.
modelAnswer: (a) Sulphur dioxide, SO₂. It turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ from orange to clear green. (b) 2CuSO₄ → 2CuO + 2SO₂ + O₂. The black residue is CuO and the neutral gas is O₂. (c) P is blue vitriol, hydrated copper(II) sulphate, CuSO₄·5H₂O. On gentle heating CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ (white X) + 5H₂O. The blue precipitate with NaOH is Cu(OH)₂, confirming Cu²⁺.

text: A white crystalline solid, on heating, crumbles with a crackling sound, leaves a yellow oxide residue and partly fuses with the glass. An acidic gas X is evolved along with a gas Y that relights a glowing splint. (a) Name the acidic gas X. (b) Write the formula of the white solid. (c) Give a chemical test to confirm gas Y.
modelAnswer: The solid is lead nitrate. It decrepitates on heating: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂. PbO is the yellow residue, and it partly fuses with the glass. (a) X is nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, a reddish-brown acidic gas. (b) The formula of the white solid is Pb(NO₃)₂. (c) Y is oxygen: a glowing splint held in the gas rekindles (bursts into flame). Oxygen is also absorbed by alkaline pyrogallol, which turns brown.
keyPoints: Y = O₂: rekindles a glowing splint

text: Priyam reacted sodium chloride with silver nitrate and obtained an insoluble salt. He filtered it and left it in a watch glass on a sunny window sill. A few hours later he noticed a change. (i) What did he observe? (ii) Why did the change occur? (iii) Give the balanced equation for this change.
modelAnswer: The insoluble salt is silver chloride: NaCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃. (i) The white precipitate turned grey/greyish-black. (ii) Silver chloride is photosensitive. Sunlight decomposes it into silver metal, which looks grey, and chlorine. This is photochemical (photolytic) decomposition. For the same reason silver salts are stored in dark coloured bottles. (iii) 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight).

text: Distinguish between: (i) exothermic and endothermic reactions (with an example of each); (ii) a drying agent and a dehydrating agent (definition).
modelAnswer: (i) An exothermic reaction releases heat, e.g. C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat, or neutralisation NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + heat. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat, e.g. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO − heat, or C + H₂O → CO + H₂ − heat (water gas). (ii) A drying agent removes moisture (free water) from a substance without reacting with it, e.g. fused CaCl₂ or quicklime. A dehydrating agent removes the elements of water (hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1) chemically from a compound, e.g. conc. H₂SO₄ turns sugar into carbon: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O.
keyPoints: Dehydrating agent removes H and O as water from a compound

text: When hydrogen is passed over a heated black solid A, a colourless liquid and a brownish-pink metal B are formed. B is divided into two test tubes; dilute HCl is added to one and dilute HNO₃ to the other. (a) Name A and B. (b) Give a chemical test for the colourless liquid. (c) What happens to A when it reacts with hydrogen? (d) Does B react with dilute HCl? Give a reason.
modelAnswer: (a) A is copper(II) oxide, CuO, and B is copper, Cu. CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. (b) The liquid is water. It turns anhydrous (white) copper sulphate blue, or blue cobalt chloride paper pink. (c) A is reduced to copper. Hydrogen removes oxygen from CuO and hydrogen itself is oxidised to water. (d) No. Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series and cannot displace hydrogen from dilute HCl. It does react with dilute nitric acid, an oxidising acid: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, giving a blue solution.
keyPoints: Water test: anhydrous CuSO₄ turns blue
Cu does not react with dilute HCl: it is below H in the activity series

text: KI + Cl₂ → KCl + I₂. (a) Balance the equation. (b) What type of reaction is it? (c) Which non-metal is less reactive? (d) What will be formed if KCl is treated with I₂?
modelAnswer: (a) 2KI + Cl₂ → 2KCl + I₂. (b) It is a displacement reaction. A more reactive (more electronegative) halogen displaces a less reactive one, and it is also a redox reaction. (c) Iodine is less reactive, because reactivity of halogens decreases down Group 17. (d) Nothing. There is no reaction, because iodine is less reactive than chlorine and cannot displace it from KCl.

text: Thin strips of metals A, B, C and D are magnesium, copper, iron and calcium respectively. (a) What is observed when: (1) an aqueous solution of the chloride of B reacts with NaOH solution; (2) moist red litmus paper is held at the mouth of the test tube in which A reacts with dilute HCl; (3) dilute H₂SO₄ is added to the carbonate of D? (b) Arrange A, B, C, D in decreasing order of reactivity. (c) Name the residue formed when C reacts with steam.
modelAnswer: (a)(1) A pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms: CuCl₂ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + 2NaCl. (a)(2) The red litmus is unchanged, because the gas is hydrogen, which is neutral: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. (a)(3) There is brisk effervescence of CO₂ at first, which slows down and stops. Sparingly soluble CaSO₄ forms a coating on the carbonate: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. (b) D (Ca) > A (Mg) > C (Fe) > B (Cu). (c) The residue is triiron tetroxide, Fe₃O₄ (magnetic oxide of iron): 3Fe + 4H₂O ⇌ Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂.
keyPoints: H₂ is neutral: no change in red litmus
CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄: reaction stops as CaSO₄ coats the carbonate

text: Write balanced equations for: (a) steam passed over red-hot iron; (b) thermal decomposition of sodium nitrate; (c) photolytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Also write the equation and one observation for the thermal decomposition of zinc nitrate.
modelAnswer: (a) 3Fe + 4H₂O ⇌ Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. (b) 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂. (c) 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (in sunlight). This is why H₂O₂ is stored in dark bottles. Zinc nitrate: 2Zn(NO₃)₂ → 2ZnO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Observation: reddish-brown fumes of NO₂ are evolved, and the residue (ZnO) is yellow when hot and white when cold.
keyPoints: 2Zn(NO₃)₂ → 2ZnO + 4NO₂ + O₂; brown fumes, residue yellow hot / white cold

text: Seema wants to differentiate between: (a) copper carbonate and zinc carbonate, by heating; (b) hard water and soft water, using soap. Explain how.
modelAnswer: (a) On heating, green copper carbonate gives a black residue (CuO): CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. White zinc carbonate gives a residue that is yellow when hot and white when cold (ZnO): ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. Both give CO₂, which turns lime water milky. (b) Shake each sample with soap solution. Soft water readily forms a rich lather. Hard water forms a white scum (an insoluble calcium/magnesium salt of the soap) and lathers only with much more soap.
keyPoints: ZnCO₃ → ZnO, yellow hot / white cold

text: Complete the table for the thermal decomposition of lead(II) nitrate: (i) name of the residue; (ii) its colour when hot; (iii) its colour when cold. Also write the equation.
modelAnswer: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂. (i) The residue is lead(II) oxide (lead monoxide, PbO). (ii) When hot it is reddish-brown (orange-red). (iii) When cold it is yellow. The salt also decrepitates (crackles), and reddish-brown NO₂ fumes are seen.

text: Dry heating of copper sulphate crystals: (a) What colour change occurs? (b) What is the source of the liquid droplets on the upper part of the test tube? (c) What is observed when a few drops of water are added to the residue? (d) Write the equation for strong heating of this residue. (e) Give a chemical test for the acidic gas evolved on strong heating.
modelAnswer: (a) The blue crystals turn into a white powder (anhydrous CuSO₄). (b) The droplets come from the water of crystallisation: CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O. (c) The white powder turns blue again and heat is evolved, as the hydrated salt reforms. (d) On strong heating anhydrous CuSO₄ decomposes: CuSO₄ → CuO + SO₃ (part of the SO₃ splits further: 2SO₃ ⇌ 2SO₂ + O₂). The residue is black CuO. (e) The gas turns moist blue litmus red. The SO₂ present turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution from orange to clear green and decolourises acidified KMnO₄.
keyPoints: Water added: white → blue, heat evolved
SO₂ turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ orange → green

text: Name the gas or gases which: (a) turn starch-iodide paper blue-black; (b) produce a brown precipitate with Nessler's reagent; (c) turn lime water milky but have no effect on acidified KMnO₄ solution.
modelAnswer: (a) Chlorine (Cl₂): Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂, and iodine turns starch blue-black. (b) Ammonia (NH₃). (c) Carbon dioxide (CO₂). SO₂ also turns lime water milky but decolourises KMnO₄.
keyPoints: CO₂: milky lime water, no effect on KMnO₄

text: With reference to the laboratory preparation of hydrogen from zinc and dilute acid: (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Why is granulated zinc used? (c) How is hydrogen collected, and why? (d) Why is the lower end of the thistle funnel dipped in the acid? (e) Why can dilute nitric acid not be used? (f) State the role of lead nitrate solution, silver nitrate solution and potassium hydroxide solution in purifying the gas.
modelAnswer: (a) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, or Zn + H₂SO₄ (dil.) → ZnSO₄ + H₂. (b) Granulated zinc has a large surface area and contains traces of impurities such as copper, which catalyse the reaction and give a steady flow. Pure zinc reacts very slowly. (c) It is collected by downward displacement of water, because hydrogen is almost insoluble in water. Collecting by air displacement would risk an explosive hydrogen–air mixture. (d) This forms a liquid seal, so hydrogen does not escape through the funnel. (e) Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and oxidises the hydrogen formed to water (and gives oxides of nitrogen). (f) Lead nitrate removes H₂S, forming a black PbS precipitate. Silver nitrate removes arsine (AsH₃) and phosphine (PH₃). KOH removes acidic gases such as SO₂ and NO₂. The gas is then dried with fused CaCl₂. Precaution: the apparatus must be airtight and kept away from flames, since a hydrogen–air mixture explodes.
keyPoints: Granulated zinc: more surface area, impurities catalyse
Thistle funnel dipped to seal the apparatus
Pb(NO₃)₂ removes H₂S; AgNO₃ removes AsH₃/PH₃; KOH removes SO₂/NO₂

text: With reference to the large-scale manufacture of hydrogen by the Bosch process: (a) Write the balanced equation (with conditions) for the preparation of water gas. (b) Write the equation (with conditions) for the reduction of steam by carbon monoxide, and name the catalyst. (c) Which gases are present along with hydrogen at the end, and how are they removed?
modelAnswer: (a) Steam is passed over red-hot coke at about 1000 °C: C + H₂O → CO + H₂. This is endothermic, and the CO + H₂ mixture is water gas. (b) Water gas mixed with excess steam is passed over a catalyst of iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) promoted with chromium(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃) at about 450 °C: CO + H₂ + H₂O → CO₂ + 2H₂. (c) CO₂ and some unreacted CO remain. CO₂ is removed by dissolving it in water under pressure (30 atm), or by absorbing it in KOH solution. The residual CO is removed by passing the gas through ammoniacal cuprous chloride solution.
keyPoints: C + H₂O → CO + H₂ (1000 °C, water gas)
CO₂ removed by water under pressure or KOH
CO removed by ammoniacal cuprous chloride

text: Give reasons: (a) Potassium (or sodium) is not used in the preparation of hydrogen from dilute acids or water. (b) Lead, though above hydrogen in the activity series, is not used to prepare hydrogen from dilute acids. (c) Copper is not used to prepare hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid.
modelAnswer: (a) Potassium and sodium react violently with acids and water. The heat produced ignites the hydrogen, which can explode, so the reaction cannot be controlled safely. (b) Lead forms an insoluble coating of PbCl₂ (with HCl) or PbSO₄ (with H₂SO₄) on its surface. The coating stops further contact with the acid and the reaction stops. (c) Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from dilute HCl.
keyPoints: Pb: insoluble PbCl₂/PbSO₄ coating stops reaction
Cu: below hydrogen in the activity series

text: Hydrogen (atomic number 1, one valence electron) is placed in Group 1 and Period 1, but it resembles both alkali metals and halogens. (a) Metal oxides can be reduced to metals by hydrogen. Which property, similar to alkali metals, is shown here? (b) Why does hydrogen form compounds like H₂O and H₂S, just as Group 1 elements form Na₂O and Na₂S? (c) Justify the statement that hydrogen is diatomic like halogens. (d) Name the ion formed by hydrogen that shows electronegative character like halogens.
modelAnswer: (a) Hydrogen acts as a reducing agent (electropositive character), like alkali metals: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. (b) Like alkali metals, hydrogen has one valence electron and valency 1. It combines with divalent oxygen and sulphur in the ratio 2:1, giving H₂O and H₂S, just as Na gives Na₂O and Na₂S. (c) Hydrogen exists as H₂ molecules, two atoms joined by a single covalent bond, just as halogens exist as Cl₂, Br₂ and so on. (d) The hydride ion, H⁻. Hydrogen gains one electron to attain the helium configuration (e.g. in NaH), just as Cl gains one to form Cl⁻.
keyPoints: Valency 1 → H₂O, H₂S like Na₂O, Na₂S

text: Differentiate between: (i) temporary hardness and permanent hardness of water (ions/salts present, and how each is removed); (ii) deliquescent and efflorescent substances (behaviour when exposed to the atmosphere).
modelAnswer: (i) Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ with HCO₃⁻). It is removed by boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂. Permanent hardness is caused by dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻). Boiling does not remove it. It is removed by adding washing soda: CaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl and MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄. (ii) Deliquescent substances absorb so much moisture from the air that they dissolve in it and form a solution, e.g. FeCl₃, CaCl₂, NaOH. They gain weight. Efflorescent substances lose their water of crystallisation to the air and crumble to a powder, e.g. washing soda and Glauber's salt. They lose weight.
keyPoints: Temporary: Ca/Mg bicarbonates, removed by boiling
Permanent: Ca/Mg chlorides and sulphates, removed by washing soda
Deliquescent: absorbs moisture, turns liquid, gains weight
Efflorescent: loses water of crystallisation, turns powdery, loses weight

text: (a) Write one advantage each of soft water and hard water. (b) Annie boiled tap water in a steel vessel for 2 hours and noticed concentric rings on the inner surface. Name the substance forming the rings, give the balanced equation for the reaction during boiling, and identify the type of hardness.
modelAnswer: (a) Soft water lathers easily with soap, saving soap, and does not form scale in boilers, kettles or pipes. Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts, which are useful minerals for bones and teeth, and it tastes better for drinking. (b) The rings are calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (with some MgCO₃), forming scale. Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂ (and Mg(HCO₃)₂ → MgCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂). The hardness removed by boiling is temporary hardness.
keyPoints: Soft water: lathers easily, no scale

text: Define: (a) water of crystallisation; (b) relative molecular mass.
modelAnswer: (a) Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules that are loosely chemically combined with a substance in its crystalline form when it crystallises from its aqueous solution. These molecules give the crystals their shape and, in some cases, their colour, e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue). (b) The relative molecular mass of a substance is the number of times one molecule of the substance is heavier than 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. It equals the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecule, e.g. H₂O = 2 + 16 = 18.
keyPoints: Fixed number of water molecules loosely combined in crystals
RMM: times heavier than 1/12 of a C-12 atom

text: (a) Define solubility. (b) A solubility curve shows the solubility of potassium nitrate and calcium sulphate at different temperatures. What can you conclude about the effect of temperature on the solubility of each? (c) Define ionisation potential.
modelAnswer: (a) Solubility of a solute at a given temperature is the maximum amount of solute, in grams, that can dissolve in 100 g of the solvent to form a saturated solution at that temperature. (b) The solubility of potassium nitrate increases sharply with rise in temperature (a steeply rising curve). The solubility of calcium sulphate decreases slightly as temperature rises (a gently falling curve), an exception to the usual trend. (c) Ionisation potential (ionisation energy) is the amount of energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom to form a positive ion.
keyPoints: Solubility: max grams of solute per 100 g solvent at a given temperature (saturated)
KNO₃ solubility rises sharply with temperature
Ionisation potential: energy to remove an outer electron from a gaseous atom

text: Define absolute zero. Why is it a theoretical concept?
modelAnswer: Absolute zero is the temperature, −273 °C or 0 K, at which the volume of a gas would theoretically become zero and its molecules would have no kinetic energy. It is only theoretical because it cannot actually be reached. All gases liquefy and then solidify before they are cooled to this temperature, so Charles' law no longer applies. A gas cannot really have zero volume, because matter occupies space.
keyPoints: Theoretical volume of gas becomes zero, no kinetic energy
Gases liquefy before reaching it, so it cannot be attained

text: Manufacturers recommend measuring tyre pressure when the tyres are cold, before a long drive. Explain using the kinetic molecular theory (KMT).
modelAnswer: During driving, friction heats the tyres and the air inside them. By KMT, a rise in temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules. They move faster and collide with the tyre walls more often and with greater force. The tyre volume is nearly fixed, so the pressure rises (P ∝ T at constant volume). A reading taken from warm tyres would therefore be higher than the true cold pressure and could lead to under-inflation. Measuring when cold gives the correct baseline value.
keyPoints: Higher temperature → higher molecular kinetic energy, more forceful collisions
At constant volume pressure rises with temperature
Cold reading gives the true pressure

text: Write balanced equations for the following: (a) KMnO₄ + HCl → KCl + MnCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂ (b) SO₂ + H₂O + HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + NO (c) HI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + H₂O + SO₂
modelAnswer: (a) 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂. Check: K 2 = 2; Mn 2 = 2; O 8 = 8; H 16 = 16; Cl 16 = 2 + 4 + 10. (b) 3SO₂ + 2H₂O + 2HNO₃ → 3H₂SO₄ + 2NO. Check: S 3 = 3; N 2 = 2; H 4 + 2 = 6 = 6; O 6 + 2 + 6 = 14 = 12 + 2. (c) 2HI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + 2H₂O + SO₂. Check: H 2 + 2 = 4 = 4; I 2 = 2; S 1 = 1; O 4 = 2 + 2.
keyPoints: Count each element on both sides to check

text: Balance the following chemical equations: (a) Fe + HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₃ + NO₂ + H₂O (b) Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + Fe (c) P + H₂SO₄ → H₃PO₄ + SO₂ + H₂O
modelAnswer: (a) Fe + 6HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₃ + 3NO₂ + 3H₂O. Check: N 6 = 3 + 3; H 6 = 6; O 18 = 9 + 6 + 3. (b) 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (thermite reaction). Check: Al 2, Fe 2, O 3 on both sides. (c) 2P + 5H₂SO₄ → 2H₃PO₄ + 5SO₂ + 2H₂O. Check: P 2 = 2; S 5 = 5; H 10 = 6 + 4; O 20 = 8 + 10 + 2.

text: Study the equation: Fe(s) + 2HCl(dil.) → FeH₂ + Cl₂(g). (a) What changes are needed to correctly represent the reaction between iron and dilute HCl? (b) What type of reaction is it? (c) Write one confirmatory test for the gas produced.
modelAnswer: (a) Iron displaces hydrogen from the acid; it does not form a hydride and chlorine is not released. The correct equation is Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), i.e. FeH₂ should be replaced by FeCl₂ (ferrous chloride) and Cl₂ by H₂. (b) It is a single (simple) displacement reaction, since iron, being above hydrogen in the reactivity series, displaces hydrogen. (c) Bring a burning splinter near the mouth of the test tube: the gas burns with a pop sound (and a pale blue flame), confirming hydrogen.
keyPoints: Hydrogen burns with a pop sound when a burning splinter is brought near

text: Write balanced chemical equations for: (a) action of heat on ferrous hydroxide (b) aluminium added to potassium hydroxide solution (c) calcium reacting with nitrogen (d) phosphorus pentoxide treated with water (e) calcium carbonate treated with dilute hydrochloric acid.
modelAnswer: (a) Fe(OH)₂ —(heat)→ FeO + H₂O. (b) 2Al + 2KOH + 2H₂O → 2KAlO₂ + 3H₂ (potassium aluminate and hydrogen are formed). (c) 3Ca + N₂ —(heat)→ Ca₃N₂ (calcium nitride). (d) P₂O₅ + 3H₂O → 2H₃PO₄ (phosphoric acid). (e) CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

text: Balance the following reactions: (a) NO₂ + H₂O + O₂ → HNO₃ (b) Al + HCl → AlCl₃ + H₂ (c) Ag₂CO₃ → Ag + CO₂ + O₂ (d) H₂S + SO₂ → H₂O + S (e) Cu + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O + SO₂
modelAnswer: (a) 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃ (N 4; H 4; O 8 + 2 + 2 = 12 = 12). (b) 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂ (Al 2; H 6; Cl 6). (c) 2Ag₂CO₃ → 4Ag + 2CO₂ + O₂ (Ag 4; C 2; O 6 = 4 + 2). (d) 2H₂S + SO₂ → 2H₂O + 3S (H 4; S 3; O 2). (e) Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + 2H₂O + SO₂ (Cu 1; H 4; S 2; O 8 = 4 + 2 + 2).

text: Write balanced chemical equations for: (i) reaction of iron with chlorine (ii) addition of silver nitrate solution to sodium chloride solution (iii) addition of zinc to sodium hydroxide solution.
modelAnswer: (i) 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ (iron(III) chloride is formed on heating iron in chlorine). (ii) AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃ (a white curdy precipitate of silver chloride). (iii) Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂↑ (on warming with concentrated NaOH, sodium zincate and hydrogen are formed).
